title: The Nun Who Would Not Stop Thinking
personName: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz

person.name: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz

shortDescription: Born in a village at the foot of the volcanoes of New Spain, Juana Inés de Asbaje y Ramírez taught herself to read before she was four, wrote a play the village performed at eight, and mastered Latin in twenty lessons. At sixteen she answered forty scholars before the viceroy's court; at seventeen she took the veil, choosing a convent for the freedom to be silent and to study. As Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz she built the largest library in New Spain, became the Tenth Muse of Europe, and answered a bishop's public rebuke with the Respuesta a Sor Filotea, the founding manifesto of Latin American feminism. For that, her superiors made her give her books away. She died in 1695 nursing her sisters through a plague. Her words are still alive.
introduction: Before she was four years old, a girl in a village at the foot of the volcanoes of New Spain taught herself to read. Before she was eight she had written a sacred play the village performed. Before she was out of her teens she had answered forty scholars in public, taken the veil, and turned a convent cell into the one place in the Spanish Empire where a woman could own ideas. The world tried three times to silence her — by refusing to teach her, by locking her behind cloistered walls, and by making her give away her books. Each time the words came back. They called her the Tenth Muse and the Phoenix of America. Three centuries later her portrait is on Mexico's currency and a university stands in the cell where her library glowed. Her name was Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, and this is the story of the mind that would not stop.

chapters.heading: The girl who taught herself to read
paragraphs: The date some records carry is 12 November 1648, though older biographers set it in 1651; even her birthday is a little exact and disputed. The place was the hacienda of San Miguel Nepantla, at the foot of the snow-capped volcanoes, on land that had belonged to the Aztec rulers and now belonged to the king of Spain. The baby was named Juana Inés de Asbaje y Ramírez. Her mother, Isabel Ramírez de Santillana, stood out among the Creole women of the region for refusing ever to marry; her father, Pedro Manuel de Asbaje, was a Basque captain who came and went across the ocean like a season. In a colony where a woman's worth was measured by her husband or her convent, a girl born to an unwed mother should have been the most quietly disposable person in the house. Her family instead noticed something strange in her, and then something unstoppable.

In the letter she would one day write about her own life, Juana said she learned to read at about three years old. Someone in the household was being taught by a woman who gave little girls their letters, and Juana begged to be taught too; whether to satisfy her or to silence her, she was taken along. Days later she could read. From then on no one could keep a book out of her hands. The hacienda of her maternal grandfather held a small library, and the girl spent her childhood hiding in the chapel so she could read its books undisturbed. When she was about eight, her family asked her to compose something for the feast of the Eucharist, and she wrote a short sacred play so accomplished that the town, in the story handed down, performed it. An aunt who heard the child declaim announced that her niece was destined for scholarship — and that nothing should keep her from it.

Her own desire to study ran into the wall every woman of the colony hit: the notion that education was wasted on a female. When she was about sixteen she asked her mother for permission to go to Mexico City dressed as a boy and sit in the classrooms of the university where no woman was admitted. Her mother refused. So the girl of the hacienda did what she would do all her life — she taught herself. She mastered Latin grammar, the language of the Church and of learning, in about twenty lessons; when she despaired at her own slowness she cut her hair, vowing that a head so empty of knowledge had no right to be dressed with any. She learned Greek logic alone, and she learned the Nahuatl of the Indigenous people around her estate as naturally as she had learned Spanish. Then her mother sent her to the capital, to her aunt's house in Mexico City, and the girl who had built one of the finest minds of her generation out of nothing but hunger walked into the grandest city of the New World.

chapters.heading: Forty learned men and one sixteen-year-old
paragraphs: Juana's wit and her evident cleverness opened the one door that was open to her. The viceroy of New Spain, Antonio Sebastián de Toledo, Marqués de Mancera, presided with his wife Leonor over a court that collected poetry the way other courts collected silver. By 1664 the sixteen-year-old had been taken into the palace itself, to serve the vicereine as a lady in waiting, and in a court that lived on verses the new girl who could compose them at speed became a phenomenon. She wrote in any form she was asked for, wrote for birthdays and victories and word games, wrote with such fluency that the court of the marqués looked at her and saw the most precocious poet of the viceroyalty. They could not yet imagine the half of it.

The test, as the story arrives to us, was arranged by the viceroy himself, who wanted to know for certain whether the young lady of the palace was what she seemed. He called together some forty of the cleverest men he could find — theologians, jurists and philosophers from the university and the cathedral — and set them the question of questions: to examine the girl publicly, as if she were taking a degree. For hours, according to the chroniclers, she stood and answered. They came at her one by one, tearing at her theses with every instrument of old and new learning, and she defended herself so fast, so calmly, and so completely that the assembled doctors were said to be as astonished as the sea looking at a warship. The comparison passed through Mexico City as a joke and then as a fact: the girl had repelled the learned men of an entire colony the way a royal galleon repels a fleet of small boats.

What next? The natural fate of a young woman of her beauty was marriage, and the natural fate of her intellect, everyone assumed, was to be folded into a husband's house like linen. She declined it, flatly, on the grounds that she did not wish to marry. The one place in the colony where a woman could keep books, make her own hours and think at full speed was a convent. In 1667 she entered the austere Carmelite convent of San José; the rigours broke her health, and within about three months she left. On 24 February 1669 she tried again and professed her vows — this time for life — in the Hieronymite order, at the Convento de San Jerónimo in the heart of Mexico City. She was seventeen, and she had, with great probability, escaped into the only freedom the colony sold to women. She took the name by which history would know her: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz.

media.caption: Sor Juana in the black habit of the Hieronymite order, in the oil painting tradition begun by Fray Miguel de Herrera.

chapters.heading: The library that frightened a bishop
paragraphs: The Convento de San Jerónimo was, in theory, a tomb of renunciation; in practice, for Sor Juana, it became a study. Into her own cell she gathered, over the years, more than four thousand books — by general agreement the largest private library in all of New Spain — along with globes, astrolabes, musical instruments and the tools of astronomer, physicist and chemist. European visitors marvelled: here was a nun who read Descartes, who quoted Aristotle in Greek, who kept the harshest critics of the Church in her room, and who, as the convent's accountant and archivist, managed its ledgers with the same exactness she brought to a sonnet. No husband, no father, no marketplace stood between her and the light. The freedom of the cell was perfect.

And out of that cell came the works that made her the greatest writer of the Spanish Baroque. The cathedrals of Mexico City, Puebla and Oaxaca commissioned her villancicos, the sung carols of feast days, and she delivered them with wit, music and theology in the same line. She wrote the long philosophical poem Primero sueño ('First Dream'), a daring nine-hundred-line voyage in which the sleeping soul ascends through the order of the universe and fails, heroically, to comprehend it — a poem about the human appetite to know, even when knowledge defeats us. She wrote El divino Narciso, a sacred play that dared to set the Christian mystery of the Eucharist beside the sacred rituals of the Aztecs, treating the native religions of her own land as something more than devilry. And she wrote comedies for the viceregal palace, love poems, satirical verses and hundreds of pieces in a voice none of her contemporaries could imitate.

Then, without her knowledge, her most splendid work got loose in the world. Her friend and protector the Countess of Paredes, a former vicereine who had carried the nun's poems out of the country when she returned to Spain, published a book of them in Madrid in 1689 — Inundación castálida. The book was a sensation. Europe, which had never heard of a woman theologian writing in the Americas, discovered a Mexican nun who was one of the finest poets of the age, and began to call her the Décima Musa, the Tenth Muse, and the Fénix de América, the Phoenix of America. A second volume was printed in Barcelona in 1692, and a third, posthumously, in Lisbon. The cloistered nun of San Jerónimo had become, without asking for it, the most famous woman of letters in the Spanish language. Fame of that size, earned by a woman, at a desk, in the colonies, attracted lightning.

media.alt: Title page of 'Inundación castálida', the first volume of Sor Juana's works, Madrid 1689
media.caption: Inundación castálida, the 1689 Madrid volume that made the cloistered nun of Mexico the Tenth Muse of Europe.

chapters.heading: The letter that started a war
paragraphs: The serene years ended in 1690. The bishop of Puebla, Don Manuel Fernández de Santa Cruz, obtained and published — without her permission — a private theological essay in which Sor Juana criticized a famous sermon by the celebrated Portuguese preacher António Vieira, and printed it under his own authority as the Carta atenagórica, the 'letter worthy of Athena.' Worse, he added an introduction signed in the name of a fictitious nun, 'Sor Filotea de la Cruz,' which praised her brilliance in the flattering voice of a sister and then, in that same loving voice, warned her that a nun who belonged to God should stop squandering her talent on profane knowledge. It was a public dressing-down delivered in your dearest friend's handwriting. New Spain understood: the most celebrated woman of the Americas had been put in her place.

Sor Juana understood it too, and she did something no one in the hierarchy had planned for. On 1 March 1691 she wrote back. Her Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz is at once an autobiography, a defense and a manifesto, and it is one of the most important documents of the colonial Americas. In pages of serene fury she told the story of the girl who had to beg for the right to read, who cut off her hair to punish herself for ignorance, who entered the convent so that she could study; she reminded her judges that a woman had taught the first Christian hero, that the church fathers had urged women to learn, that wisdom was a gift of God that God had never reserved for men alone. About the scholars who mocked women's studies she wrote the phrase that outlived the bishop: 'What can women know but the philosophies of the kitchen?' — and answered her own mockery: 'If Aristotle had known how to cook, he would have written a great deal more.'

The letter is careful, literate and merciless. She explained that she studied not for applause but, in her own words, 'only to see whether, by studying, I may come to know less poorly'; and she answered the charge that her appetite for knowledge was a vanity with the confession that it was the one hunger that was not a sin. She knew to the letter what the cost would be. The church had no interest in receiving the theological challenge; it had asked for surrender. Under pressure from her confessor, the severe Jesuit Antonio Núñez de Miranda, and the archbishop of Mexico, who had once declared he would rather see a woman never learn to read, Sor Juana stopped writing around 1693. In 1694 she sold or gave away her library — the four thousand volumes that were her life's work — giving the money to the poor, together with her instruments and her music. And she signed a formal renunciation in her own blood: 'I, the worst of all — the worst woman in the world.'

media.alt: 'Hombres necios', Sor Juana's satirical poem, printed in an early edition of her works
media.caption: In an early edition of her works: 'Hombres necios que acusáis' — the verse that mocked, in rhyme, the double standard that punished her in life.

chapters.heading: The plague, the death, and the voice that refused to die
paragraphs: She had little more than a year of silence. In 1695 a violent epidemic of matlazahuatl, a typhus-like fever no one could cure, fell upon Mexico City and upon the Convento de San Jerónimo with particular cruelty. Sor Juana did the only thing her order allowed her to do, and did it as she did everything: completely. She nursed her sick sisters day and night, emptying cells, folding fever-soaked sheets, reciting the offices of the dying. She caught the disease herself. On 17 April 1695, at the age of forty-six, she died, as the church record dryly notes, 'of the epidemic that afflicted this convent.' When her cell was opened it contained, by the same record, an unfinished poem and a few coins. That is all the world got back of the four thousand books.

If her life had ended there, it would still be one of the great stories of the world: the outcast girl who read her way to the summit of a civilization and then was returned to dirt by it. But the story has an ending her enemies did not plan. She had been silenced, yet her words had been printed in Madrid, in Barcelona and in Lisbon, and books, once printed, are ageless and careless of obedience. In 1700, five years after her death, the posthumous collection Fama y obras póstumas appeared in Lisbon — and it contained the Respuesta, the very letter that had been meant as the instrument of her humiliation. Europe, which had already chosen her for its Tenth Muse, now held in its hands the sound of her defiance. Century after century, while the men who condemned her were forgotten even in Puebla, her books were read; and every woman in the Spanish-speaking world who wrote with a brain and a body was afterwards measured against the woman who had said it first, and better.

Three centuries on, no one in her country doubts the outcome of the war she did not ask for and could not lose. The Convento de San Jerónimo, the prison she turned into a library, is today the Universidad del Claustro de Sor Juana, standing on the exact ground where her books stood. Her face is on the two-hundred-peso banknote of Mexico, and every schoolchild knows by heart the redondilla 'Hombres necios que acusáis' — 'foolish men, who blame women without reason.' Octavio Paz, the Nobel laureate, devoted a biography to her, The Traps of Faith. Scholars call the Respuesta the founding document of Latin American feminism. And the last word still belongs to her, in the letter written to bury her: they could take her books, her instruments and her silence, but they could not touch the part of her that refused to stop thinking — and is still refusing, four centuries later, on the currency of her country.

chapters.heading: The desire that could not be confiscated
paragraphs: The most quietly subversive sentence Sor Juana ever wrote is in plain sight inside the Respuesta. Recounting how she learned to read, the woman who defeated forty scholars wrote that she came to her letters, absurdly, from the very first 'because I desired to know.' She made the desire sound as natural and as innocent as thirst. Everything else — the Latin cut into her own hair, the convent chosen as a library with a veil attached, the four thousand volumes, the verses of the Tenth Muse — was only that first desire, disguised and saving itself, refuge to refuge. And the desire itself was the whole argument. Every authority of her world told her a woman's mind was a vanity to be policed. She answered with one unassailable fact: I desired to know, and I went and did it, and it did not damn me, and the world is richer for it.

It is easy, from the safe distance of centuries, to reduce her to a saint or a victim, and to let the famous blood signature — 'the worst of all' — close the book on her as a tragedy. But the biography insists on being read the other way. She was not defeated; she was slowly burned by the fear of small men, and she took the blows, and died nursing others, and left the strongest words in the language on the shelf. The library was taken away; the words were not. The labour of her life was never the accumulation of books that could be sold; it was the building of a mind that could not be. And that mind outlasted the convent, outlasted the empire that built the viceroyalty, outlasted the bishop of Puebla, and is present today in every classroom where a girl is shown that the world's knowledge was never once reserved for men.

Mexico remembers her with the titles that were once a wonder and are now a coronation: the Tenth Muse, the Phoenix of America, the woman who was reading before anyone told her she was allowed to, and whose last act on earth was to hold the hand of a dying sister while an epidemic that no one understood took her in turn. Her cell is a museum now, the room in which the largest library in New Spain once glowed. On the day she died, someone went in and found an unfinished poem and a few coins. Three centuries later the unfinished poem is printed in every anthology of the Spanish language, the coins are not, and the world still has not finished listening. She desired to know. That is the whole story, and there has never been a finer one.
